items.title: [c-jcm.com] Cancer AI studies report support benefits, high accuracy and readability gaps
items.content_html: A study of 140 patients with pancreatic cancer found that those who used an AI assistant’s psychological-support feature had lower anxiety and quality-of-life scores than nonusers. More frequent overall use was also associated with lower anxiety, but the relationship was borderline statistically significant. Researchers assessed patients once in April and May 2026; the findings show an association, not that the tool caused the differences. Separate lung-cancer research found high accuracy in AI answers to patient questions, but all three systems tested produced text at a 10th- to 12th-grade reading level. Other cancer studies presented for a pathology meeting reported on AI applications for classifying tumors, drafting molecular reports and deciding when rapid testing could be deferred.

items.title: [scimex.org] Astronomers trace eight-minute radio pulses to white dwarf and Sun-like star
items.content_html: Astronomers have traced repeating radio pulses from the system GPM J071507−114153 to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star—the first known long-period radio transient with this type of stellar pairing. The pulses recur every 7.9 minutes but appear only during a roughly six-hour window in each 32-hour orbit. The system lies more than 5,000 light-years away. Researchers discovered the system using Australia’s Murchison Widefield Array, pinpointed it with South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope and used the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to identify the companion as a G-type star. Measurements of the orbit and the companion’s slight movement indicate that the pulsing object has about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, making it too light to be a neutron star. The study was published in Nature Astronomy on Nov. 12, 2026.

items.title: [dlr.de] Europe’s Hera probe reveals Didymos ridge as asteroid-defense survey begins
items.content_html: The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has begun its close study of the Didymos asteroid pair. New images show boulders, craters and a sharply defined ridge around Didymos’ equator. Hera is inspecting the system after NASA deliberately struck its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, in 2022 to test asteroid deflection. The images, taken from about 56 kilometers away, show a side of Didymos that NASA’s DART spacecraft did not see before impact. Scientists say Didymos’ rapid spin may help explain the ridge and could send surface material toward its equator or into space. Hera will continue its survey with 25 instruments. Two CubeSats are due to investigate Dimorphos at closer range, including with radar and an attempted landing. The agency plans to release detailed images of both asteroids on Nov. 25.

items.title: [universetoday.com] Chandra links recurring stellar outbursts to hidden compact companion
items.content_html: Astronomers say AT 2016blu, in the galaxy NGC 4559 about 30 million light-years away, is not a supernova but a massive star whose repeated outbursts likely involve a black hole or neutron-star companion. The star has survived 27 recorded outbursts recurring roughly every 113 days since 2012. An observation by the Chandra X-ray Observatory timed to an outburst in March 2026 found the star was 100 times brighter in X-rays than in observations from 2001-02. Researchers say the companion draws in gas shed by the star during close orbital approaches, and the gas heats up and emits X-rays. They estimate that gas equivalent to about 2.7% of Earth’s mass transfers to the companion during each outburst.

items.title: [newscientist.com] Independent analysis confirms ring in M87* black hole image
items.content_html: An independent reanalysis of Event Horizon Telescope observations has reproduced the bright ring surrounding the black hole's shadow in the first black hole image, confirming the central feature of the 2019 image of M87*. The study, published Nov. 11 in Nature, used a separate imaging method to address questions about whether image-processing choices had produced the ring. The team, led by CSIRO astronomers Samuel Lai and Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, analyzed observations from 2017, 2018 and 2021. The ring in the new images had an average diameter of 42.2 microarcseconds, consistent with an estimated black hole mass of 6.5 billion solar masses. The researchers said the result supports the ring-like shape predicted by general relativity, although fine details such as ring thickness and brightness distribution still vary with the method and data quality.

items.title: [zmescience.com] Mantle-driven uplift explains Earth's billion-year rock gap, study finds
items.content_html: A new model suggests slow circulation in Earth’s mantle lifted parts of three ancient continental regions, allowing ice sheets to erode rock layers and create the Great Unconformity, a gap in the geological record. The study by University of Wollongong researchers Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament was published Nov. 4 in Nature. The model indicates Laurentia, Baltica and North China rose from roughly a billion years ago to about 540 million years ago, then began sinking, allowing younger sediments to accumulate. Flament said glaciation likely drove much of the erosion, but mantle uplift created the slopes glaciers needed to carry sediment away.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
items.content_html: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.

items.title: [space.com] Simulations link Uranus and Neptune’s skewed magnetic fields to interior conditions
items.content_html: Computer simulations based on Voyager 2 measurements suggest that increasing electrical conductivity with depth inside Uranus and Neptune may explain their unusually tilted, off-center magnetic fields. The study, led by Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin, was published Nov. 3 in Communications Physics. The models indicate that the fields may also shift substantially over decades, unlike Earth’s comparatively steady magnetic tilt. Researchers are using observations of faint auroras from the James Webb Space Telescope to track the planets’ magnetic environments; NASA has prioritized a Uranus mission for the early 2040s.

items.title: [science.nasa.gov] NASA studies show LISA could detect planets through gravitational waves
items.content_html: Two studies led by NASA astrophysicists describe how the planned Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) could detect exoplanets orbiting pairs of white dwarfs through the planets’ effects on gravitational-wave signals. Such detections would reveal a population not yet observed: planets around binary white dwarfs. LISA is scheduled to launch in the mid-2030s, and researchers estimate the Milky Way contains about 10 million double-white-dwarf systems with orbital periods under an hour. The studies also describe how NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope could help verify candidate planets. The findings appeared in The Astrophysical Journal.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🪶 🌲 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html: Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Stanford researchers use brain scans to flag Alzheimer’s risk years earlier
items.content_html: Stanford Medicine researchers developed an MRI-based score that identified brain activity patterns linked to later cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease, potentially before memory problems or established biomarkers appear. The researchers developed the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome (ARC) score by comparing brain scans taken at rest from 180 adults over 75 with unusually strong memory and 110 people diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. They then tested it in more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults aged 55 to 70. During up to 12 years of follow-up, participants with more Alzheimer’s-like patterns experienced faster cognitive decline and were more likely to develop amyloid plaques or receive a diagnosis. The researchers say the score is neither a diagnosis nor a certain prediction for an individual. They are planning a trial to test whether cognitive training can change ARC scores.

items.title: [science.nasa.gov] Chandra traces giant star’s 113-day eruptions to black hole or neutron star
items.content_html: NASA astronomers say the Chandra X-ray Observatory has identified a hidden companion that appears to trigger repeated eruptions from AT 2016blu, a giant star in the galaxy NGC 4559, about 30 million light-years away. The star, estimated to have at least 33 times the Sun’s mass, brightens and dims in bursts that resemble supernovae but do not destroy it. The companion is either a black hole or a neutron star, pulling material from AT 2016blu every 113 days as the pair approach each other in their orbit. Chandra recorded the star as at least 100 times brighter in X-rays in March 2026 than in observations from 2001 and 2002, supporting the explanation that captured material heats up and emits X-rays. The findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal.
